hints: Look at the light grey bars for Na to Cl and think about what is added to the atom as proton number increases across the period.
Think about whether the extra electrons go into a new shell or the same shell, and what this means for shielding.
walkthrough:
Picture what changes across the period**
Moving from Na to Cl you add one proton and one electron at each step. The key idea is that all those outer electrons go into the same third shell, the 3s then 3p, so there is no new inner shell to block the extra nuclear charge.

Link nuclear charge to pull**
Proton number rises from 11 to 17, so nuclear charge gets larger while shielding stays roughly constant. That means the effective pull on each outer electron gets stronger, drawing the whole electron cloud in closer and making the atom smaller.

Final answer: Atomic radius decreases due to increasing attraction between nucleus and outer electrons.
Nuclear charge increases across the period with similar shielding as electrons are added to the same outer shell.

hints: Compare the electron arrangement of Na atom, $2,8,1$, with $\text{Na}^{+}$, and think about which shell is now the outer shell.
walkthrough:
See what is lost when the cation forms**
Na to Si form positive ions by losing all their 3rd shell electrons. $\text{Na}$ is $2,8,1$ but $\text{Na}^{+}$ is $2,8$. $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is $2,8$, $\text{Al}^{3+}$ is $2,8$, $\text{Si}^{4+}$ is $2,8$. The whole n=3 shell has gone, so the outer electrons are now in n=2, much closer to the nucleus, and fewer electrons are held by the same or greater nuclear charge.
Final answer: Ions of Na to Si have lost the outer shell / outer electrons, so the ion has one fewer shell than the atom and greater effective nuclear charge on the remaining electrons.

hints: Recall how $\text{P}^{3-}$, $\text{S}^{2-}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ are formed from P, S and Cl, and whether a shell is lost or kept.
Think about what happens to repulsion when extra electrons are squeezed into the same outer shell with the same number of protons.
walkthrough:
Picture anion formation**
P, S and Cl gain electrons to fill the 3p sub-shell. $\text{P}$ becomes $\text{P}^{3-}$, $\text{S}$ becomes $\text{S}^{2-}$, $\text{Cl}$ becomes $\text{Cl}^{-}$. No shell is lost, the outer shell stays as n=3, but there are now more electrons in it.

Feel the extra repulsion**
The nuclear charge has not changed, but there are more negative electrons repelling each other in the same space. That extra electron-electron repulsion pushes the cloud outwards, so the anion is larger than its atom.

Final answer: P to Cl form ions by gaining electrons into the same outer shell / p sub-shell.
Increased repulsion between electrons in the same / outer shell causes the electron cloud to expand.

hints: Write the outer electron arrangements for Mg, $\text{3s}^{2}$, and Al, $\text{3s}^{2}\text{3p}^{1}$, and identify which electron is removed in each case.
Compare the distance, shielding and energy of a 3p electron with a 3s electron.
walkthrough:
Spot which electron leaves**
Mg is $1\text{s}^{2}2\text{s}^{2}2\text{p}^{6}3\text{s}^{2}$. The first ionisation removes a 3s electron. Al is $1\text{s}^{2}2\text{s}^{2}2\text{p}^{6}3\text{s}^{2}3\text{p}^{1}$. The first ionisation removes the single 3p electron.

Compare 3p with 3s**
The 3p orbital is slightly further out on average and is shielded by the filled 3s electrons as well as the inner shells. It is higher in energy, so less energy is needed to remove it despite the higher nuclear charge of Al. That is why Al dips below Mg.

Final answer: Outer electron removed from Al is in a 3p subshell / orbital, whereas for Mg it is in 3s.
The 3p electron is higher in energy / more shielded / further from the nucleus and so removed more easily.

hints: Write the 3p arrangements for P, $\text{3p}^{3}$, and S, $\text{3p}^{4}$, and think about how the electrons are arranged in the three p orbitals.
Consider what happens when two electrons have to share the same p orbital in sulfur.
walkthrough:
Draw the p boxes in your head**
P is $3\text{p}^{3}$ with one electron in each p orbital, all unpaired. S is $3\text{p}^{4}$, so one orbital must contain a pair: $\uparrow\downarrow$, $\uparrow$, $\uparrow$. The first ionisation of S removes one electron from that pair.

Use repulsion to explain the dip**
Two electrons sharing the same orbital repel each other strongly. That pair repulsion partly cancels the extra nuclear charge in S, so the paired electron comes off more easily and S has a lower first ionisation energy than P.

Final answer: Outer electron for S is paired in a p orbital / S has one doubly occupied p orbital whereas P has three singly occupied p orbitals.
Spin-pair / electron-pair repulsion makes the paired electron easier to remove.

hints: Write the formulae $\text{NaCl}$, $\text{MgCl}_{2}$, $\text{AlCl}_{3}$, $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ and work out the oxidation number of the Period 3 element in each.
Link the oxidation number to the group number and the number of outer shell electrons lost or shared.
Think about the oxidation number of chlorine in each chloride and whether it changes.
walkthrough:
Calculate the metal oxidation numbers**
With $\text{Cl}$ as $-1$, $\text{NaCl}$ gives Na as $+1$, $\text{MgCl}_{2}$ gives Mg as $+2$, $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ gives Al as $+3$, $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ gives Si as $+4$. So the value rises by one each step from Na to Si.

Explain with outer electrons**
Na has 1 outer electron, Mg has 2, Al has 3, Si has 4. Each element uses all its outer electrons in bonding to chlorine, either by loss or sharing, so the formula contains 1, 2, 3, 4 chlorines respectively, matching the group number.

Fix chlorine**
In every case chlorine only needs one electron to complete its octet, so its oxidation number stays at $-1$ throughout.

Final answer: Oxidation number of Na to Si increases from +1 to +4 / by 1 each time.
This is due to increasing number of valence electrons used, $\text{NaCl}$, $\text{MgCl}_{2}$, $\text{AlCl}_{3}$, $\text{SiCl}_{4}$, number of chlorines matches group number.
Chlorine oxidation number is -1 in all / stays the same.

hints: For sodium chloride think about a physical change where the lattice breaks into mobile ions, no new covalent bonds form.
For silicon(IV) chloride think about a vigorous chemical reaction with water that produces white fumes of hydrogen chloride and a solid oxide.
walkthrough:
Dissolve NaCl**
$\text{NaCl}$ is ionic. Water simply separates the lattice into hydrated ions. No bonds to hydrogen or oxygen are made in a chemical sense, so write a dissolution equation: $$\text{NaCl} \rightarrow \text{Na}^{+} + \text{Cl}^{-}$$ State symbols $\text{(s)}$, $\text{(aq)}$ are acceptable.

Hydrolyse $\text{SiCl}_{4}$**
$\text{SiCl}_{4}$ is covalent and hydrolysed violently by water to give white solid silicon dioxide and steamy fumes of $\text{HCl}$: $$\text{SiCl}_{4} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{SiO}_{2} + 4\text{HCl}$$ Check balance: 1 Si, 4 Cl, 4 H, 2 O on both sides.

Final answer: sodium chloride: $\text{NaCl} \rightarrow \text{Na}^{+} + \text{Cl}^{-}$
silicon(IV) chloride: $\text{SiCl}_{4} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{SiO}_{2} + 4\text{HCl}$

hints: Recall the melting point and conductivity of $\text{NaCl}$ and what type of lattice gives those properties.
Recall that $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ is a volatile liquid and think about what structure gives low melting point.
walkthrough:
Classify sodium chloride**
$\text{NaCl}$ is a high melting solid that conducts when molten. That points to strong electrostatic attraction in all directions. So structure is giant ionic lattice and bonding is ionic.

Classify silicon(IV) chloride**
$\text{SiCl}_{4}$ is a liquid with low boiling point made of discrete $\text{SiCl}_{4}$ units held by weak van der Waals forces. So structure is simple molecular and bonding within each molecule is covalent.

Final answer: sodium chloride, structure: giant / lattice / ionic; bonding: ionic.
silicon(IV) chloride, structure: simple / molecular; bonding: covalent.
